components.gap: Success condition requires the identified source variants to be preserved; not met for the sum system. The source's own S2 (journal p. 357 eqs (46)-(48), p. 358 eqs (50)-(51)): Delta = theta(1-alpha)^(1/2), obtained from its eq. (47) P{E in A2(theta)|theta} = 1-(Delta/theta)^2, so the band is theta(1-(1-alpha)^(1/2)) <= x1+x2 <= theta(1+(1-alpha)^(1/2)) and the limits are S/(1+(1-alpha)^(1/2)), S/(1-(1-alpha)^(1/2)). This is neither reproduced nor recorded. Under the 'Example I' heading, body lines 30, 39 and 43 instead display a different band, qt <= S <= (2-q)t, with half-width (1-q)t and I2=[S/(2-q),S/q], and give no note of the change. The two systems coincide only at alpha=3/4. For every other alpha, the displayed 'three systems' are not the source's three systems. This is an unrecorded substitution of a different regime, and the presentation implies it is the source's system. The handbook mathematics is correct; what is missing is any record of the source's printed system and its deviation. The boundary changes in A1 and A3 (the source has strict inequalities) are recorded only generically, at lines 44-46.

defect_observations.observation: Single root cause of the three partial verdicts: the held source's eq. (47) on journal p. 357 miscalculates P(theta-Delta <= S <= theta+Delta) as 1-(Delta/theta)^2. The correct value is 1-(1-Delta/theta)^2. As a result the source's printed S2, eqs (48) and (50)-(53), does not have coverage alpha unless alpha=3/4; a Monte Carlo check gives about 0.914 at alpha=0.5 and about 0.397 at alpha=0.95. The handbook uses the corrected band but nowhere records the source's printed version, its error, or that every alpha=3/4 comparison in the source is unaffected. A grep of body and annex finds no mention of the source's eqs (47)-(53).

The source's own boundary assignment is not stated. Its eq. (93) puts x1 = theta1/2 in the upper branch, and eq. (94) has the strict bound x2 < alpha(theta1-x1). Under that printed assignment the inverted set is empty when alpha<1/2 and alpha <= v/u < 1-alpha; for example alpha=3/10 and v/u in {3/10, 1/2, 13/20} were checked by exact scan. It is open when v/u < min(alpha, 1-alpha); for example alpha=1/2 and v/u=1/4 give (1.5u, 2u). This contradicts the source's statement on p. 369 that the regions 'may serve as regions of acceptance' (conditions (ii) and (iv) on p. 354). The handbook only says that a boundary completion is 'required' (lines 12-13 and 227) and does not record the source's version. Treated as recorded generically, so it is not a failure.

The source's eq. (89) has the strict lower inequality b(theta1-x1) < x2, which makes the theta-interval half-open and so fails condition (iv) literally. The handbook closes it, and the change is recorded only through the global 'All interval endpoints below are included' at line 12.

The terms 'marginally relevant z' and 'every relevant z' are not defined. The marginal m_{theta,eta} depends on the nuisance value, so the definition does not say for which eta the conditional density and the alpha-section requirement must hold. Annex lines 112-113 read the term as m_{theta,eta}(z) > 0, and the combination step at annex lines 130-133 needs the section identity m_{t,eta}-a.e. for every eta.

The source's Proposition X is cited only as the result whose obstruction is 'underlying' the handbook's theorem. Its hypotheses are not stated: continuity in W, a continuous theta-derivative 'not identically equal to zero', differentiation under the integral over W, and hypothesis (3), a boundary point of A(theta') with p(E|theta') != 0. Its conclusion form is also absent: a third value theta''' and a region B satisfying eqs (102)-(103). The contrasts drawn at body lines 354-356 and annex lines 573-578 refer to these only implicitly.

The upper one-sided optimum is proved by 'the same argument' (lines 631-635). The differing premise, a decreasing likelihood ratio, and the resulting region are both stated, so the treatment was accepted. The Neyman-Pearson lemma (thm:p15-neyman-pearson in hypothesis-tests-and-confidence.tex line 95) and the 'normal transformation theorem' are invoked without cross-references.
Notation clash within one chapter: q = sqrt(1-alpha) in Example I (line 24), while q is the slope of the ray v = qu in the switched comparison (lines 247-250), following the source's eq. (95).

'The conditional first-coordinate distribution has no atoms' is asserted without the one-line reason that a Lebesgue density gives hyperplanes probability zero; the endpoint cases 'follow by limits'. Both are compressed but immaterial to coverage.
